pageCache.text:
Welcome to our website
We are very proud of the community we have here at Cottesmore St Mary. It is very consciously modeled on the communities of the early Christians. Those early Christians tried to live their lives according to the teaching and example of Jesus, their friend.
They met together to talk about Jesus and all he taught them (we call this sharing the Word), they met together to pray (Worship), they showed others how he wanted us to live (they gave Witness) and they looked after each other (they cared about the Welfare of all).
This model underpins our Mission statement and our Values, through which we endeavour to provide the best education for each child in our school as we guide them towards discovery of their own unique set of God given talents.
We are a community of learners. We have high standards of our children with regards to all they do and, in return, we strive to give them the very best of what we can offer. We pride ourselves on our relationships with families and always operate an open door policy.
We hope our website gives you a glimpse of how we work together as a Catholic community to ensure our Vision is met.
We want the children who leave our school to make the most of every learning opportunity so that they can grow into the best people they can be, fulfilling their dreams and God’s special plan for them, being happy and confident and joyfully showing to others their faith in God.
Our school is a popular two form Catholic primary school and we hope that, if you come to visit us, you will sense what a wonderful place it is.
We look forward to meeting you.

Governors
Welcome from the Chair of Governors
In Autumn 2024, Thomas Medveczky and Katie Raymond were appointed as Co-Chair of Governors.
As the Governing Body we are responsible for the School’s strategy, finances , policies and ensuring that the School follows the Catholic ethos. There is an expectation for all governors to visit the school during the year to become familiar with school improvement priorities e.g. follow up staff presentations on curriculum development, equality, behaviour and learning. Governors also place a high priority on communicating with the school community and attend parent/teacher evenings and other school events, including the annual summer fair.
There is a high priority for Governors and the Diocese to attend training sessions organised by Brighton & Hove Local Authority to ensure they are able to carry out their role effectively.
We welcome you to Cottesmore and believe your child will enjoy every aspect of their time at the school and will be a valued member of our school community.
Katie Raymond and Dr Thomas Medveczky
To contact our governors you can email: clerk@cottesmore.brighton-hove.sch.uk
The four Primary Committees that meet are:
Finance & Personnel
Curriculum and Standards
Pupils, Parents and Community
Admissions
The Secondary Committees are
Headteacher's Appraisal
Pupil Premium
Training and Development
Parent Forum
Pupil Discipline
Ofsted Working Party

Grace Allemany-Liley ( Staff Governor )
I am delighted to be part of the Board of the Governors at Cottesmore as one of the Foundation Governors, appointed by the Bishop.
I have moved to Brighton in 2005, where I have been practicing Medicine as a Doctor in most of the local hospitals across Sussex. I am a Consultant Physician specialising in Respiratory Medicine, and also provide leadership and oversight of medical services that the NHS runs in the community in Sussex.
I hope that with my experience of frontline medicine, leading large-scale change projects and service development, I can help Cottesmore to thrive and be ready for the future. My oldest attends Cottesmore, so you will see me at various school activities.
Frances van Berkel
I am delighted to have been appointed as Foundation Governor for Cottesmore St Mary’s. I have had a long association with the school as my 5 children all attended there before going on to Cardinal Newman and, bolstered by such good education, into successful careers.
I taught English in Secondary schools for many years and also taught for a few years at Cottesmore before going on to become an independent Education Consultant. I hope to use all that experience to support the school in my role as Governor on the Curriculum and Standards Committee.
I am a parishioner at The Sacred Heart where I sing in the choir and was also a Catechist for many years. I am committed to supporting the Catholic ethos of the school and using my skills and experience as the new chair of the Admissions Committee.
Cian Cronin
I am a Foundation Governor at Cottesmore St Mary and a parent of two children currently attending the school. It is a privilege to support the school community both as a governor and as a parent.
Professionally, I work as a Director in a consultancy advising local authorities on housing, regeneration and property strategy. I previously held a senior director role within a local authority, where I was responsible for town planning, economic development, property, asset management and strategic development. This experience has given me a strong understanding of governance, financial oversight and long-term planning within the public sector, which I hope to bring to my role on the governing body.
As a Foundation Governor, I am committed to supporting the Catholic ethos of the school and ensuring that every child is able to flourish academically, socially and spiritually in a nurturing and ambitious environment. I look forward to contributing to the continued success of Cottesmore St Mary.
Jane Cross
I was appointed as a Foundation Governor in June 2024.
For many years I lived in West Sussex and worked as a professional property lawyer; fifteen years ago I moved to Hove and completely changed direction obtaining an arts based degree.
I have 2 adult children and fully supported them throughout their education. I now have the opportunity to support my two grandchildren who attend Cottesmore. I wish to contribute to the school in any way I can and already attend many functions. I can be found most days shepherding my grandchildren through the playground. Please stop me as I am always happy to listen.
Arthur Gallagher ( Associate Governor)
Arthur resigned as a foundation governor but was re-appointed as an Associate Governor in Autumn 2024. His role is primarily to assist with the question of Academisation but also to provide knowledge and advice into the handovers of Chair of Governors and Chair of F&P. He attends some committee meetings, but has no voting rights at all in any meeting.
We no longer have primary school children, as ours have grown to Cardinal Newman and beyond. However as a parishioner of the Sacred Heart I'm delighted to have the opportunity to support this great local catholic school. I have been involved with this governing board since Autumn 2015 and the role gives me an excellent opportunity to apply my professional skills to help the school. Not only can I contribute to building a better foundation for young members of our community, but in the process I can also extend my own personal experience and faith. I have gained experience in various committees, panels, working parties and partnerships, and I am happy to chair the Finance and Personnel committee. As Vice Chair of the board I also enjoy supporting our chair and our very capable headteacher. I look forward to developing our leadership, putting the school into an ever-stronger position to support our staff as they nurture our pupils and help them to achieve in and enjoy their life ahead.
Peter Gwilliam
I am retired from a career teaching Mathematics in Secondary Schools, largely to A-Level students. I also held a range of management jobs. In that time I have been a teacher governor twice and a governor of Fairlight School. I am a parishioner of St Josephs Church. My son attended Cardinal Newman School for 5 years.
I still want to be of service in education and so applied to be a Local Authority governor. I am very pleased to have been appointed to the governing body of Cottesmore St Mary. I hope that my experience in education will support and help to guide the school to continue its wonderful performance.
Maz Gzybovska
I moved to Brighton in 2005 to study Economics at Sussex University and currently work for a local financial organisation. My professional focus has been transformation and change delivery across all areas of the business. Both of my children attend Cottesmore and having seen how well the school is run I decided I'd like to contribute in a more dedicated capacity, especially given the recent challenges that we've all had to overcome due to global pandemic. I am keen to use my professional experience and skills as a member of Financial & Personnel Committee and chair of Admissions Committee.
Dr Thomas Medveczky ( Co-Chair of Governors )
I am delighted to be part of the Board of the Governors at Cottesmore as one of the Foundation Governors, appointed by the Bishop.
I have moved to Brighton in 2005, where I have been practicing Medicine as a Doctor in most of the local hospitals across Sussex. I am a Consultant Physician specialising in Respiratory Medicine, and also provide leadership and oversight of medical services that the NHS runs in the community in Sussex.
I hope that with my experience of frontline medicine, leading large-scale change projects and service development, I can help Cottesmore to thrive and be ready for the future. My oldest attends Cottesmore, so you will see me at various school activities.
Alex Melhuish
Originally from Cardiff, Alex is a Year 4 teacher in Portslade with a career rooted in social justice and advocacy. After earning a degree in Social Policy and a Master's in Social Documentation, he balanced roles as a researcher for the National Evaluation of Sure Start and a camera technician in film and TV, eventually producing his own documentary.
Alex's dedication to youth welfare was further shaped by his work as a youth worker supporting victims of violence at King's College and St George's hospitals in London.
Now specialising in primary education with a PGCE, Alex leads Anti-Racist Education at his school. He is set to join the Board of Governors as the Anti-Racism and Racial Literacy Lead, motivated by a desire to support the community and the school his two children attend.
Jessica Moore
Having been connected with Cottesmore St Mary’s since 2019, when my eldest son began Year 2, the school has become an integral part of our family’s life. I was therefore very pleased to be elected as a Parent Governor in July 2025, just as my youngest son was about to begin his own journey at the school.
As both a parent and a professional with a background in Human Resources, Education, and Mental Health, I am passionate about supporting environments where children, staff, and families can thrive and reach their full potential. In my role as Parent Governor, I look forward to contributing my skills, experience, and perspective to help guide the continued growth and development of the school in the years ahead.
Katie Raymond ( Co-Chair of Governors )
I joined as a Governor in Autumn 2020 to help support the school Governing Body. I am originally from Bromley and moved to Brighton and Hove in 2002 to train and qualify as a solicitor after finishing my English and Music degree in Leeds and my post-graduate qualifications in London. I have worked in several law firms in our local area, and am now a Real Estate Partner at a large regional firm, based in their Brighton office. In addition to my role as Co-Chair, I chair the Curriculum Committee. My older son is at Cardinal Newman and my younger son is at Cottesmore. If you have any issues or questions about the governing board, please do speak to me.
Dr Catherine Williamson
I have spent many years locally in education. I was trained to teach secondary RE and subsequently went to the University of Brighton’s School of Education where I taught on the Initial Teacher Training course for both primary and secondary RE.
I delivered the Catholic Certificate in Religious Studies for many years at the University and University Chaplaincy. I have also spent many years as a parish catechist. I am now retired. My four children all attended Cottesmore.
Caroline Thoms

pageCache.pageTitle: Music | Cottesmore St Mary Catholic Primary School
pageCache.text:
Music
MUSIC
INTENT
To develop musical understanding in all pupils and promote a lifelong love of music. To develop all children as young musicians with confidence in their singing and instrumental performance. To develop knowledge of music from a wide variety different cultures and musical periods. To present a diverse selection of music and musicians through which the children will discover their own musical preferences.
IMPLEMENTATION
This is achieved through the teaching of high quality music lessons that are centered on learning to perform using instruments and singing. Learning music also includes appraising and composing. These strands are made relevant to the children by being related to the musical performance (instrument or style) being taught during a lesson.
A spiral instrumental curriculum is implemented with children gradually increasing their depth of knowledge and instrumental skills as they return to instruments at an older age. By year 6 children will be able to choose their own instruments to perform in mixed ensembles. Children are encouraged to have their own instruments (ukulele and recorders) to extend their learning at home, and use throughout their time at school.
Singing is an integral part of the music curriculum and included in each music lesson. A Kodály based approach is used to build up singing and aural skills from a young age using simple folk based melodies. Singing is expanded upon in a weekly hymn assembly for KS1 and KS2. Singing and listenning is embedded in the classroom with repertoire shared by the Music Lead with teachers.
Composition is taught as an interlinked part of musical performance. Children will be taught a model style of music performance, before using these skills to produce their own musical compositions or improvisations.
Notation is taught as a tool for musical performance and is secondary to musical outcomes. Sound is taught before symbol, so that when encountering notation children understand its purpose. Notation is only used when it is culturally appropriate for the music being learnt.
Sequencing Music is taught internally first (using voice and body) before using external sounds (instruments). Learning is sequenced, where possible, to learn Rhythmic instruments before moving on to Melodic instruments. We use a spiral curriculum with instrumental skills being re-visted throughout the curriculum, giving pupils the chance to build up in depth musical skills at particular instruments.
Appraising is used as an integral part of music lessons with listening repertoire chosen from a wide variety of sources including music of non-western cultures, classical music, pop and rock styles. Care is taken to show performers from BAME and a balance of genders.
When choosing material to teach, musical learning and skill development always takes precedence over a link current school topics.
Technology is integrated into the music classroom and used whenever appropriate. Seesaw is used as a tool for setting and recording pupils work and extending learning to the home. Video and audio recordings allow pupils to reflect on their own work. Children use recording and technology such as Garageband to develop their music composition skills.
Assessment of skills and progression is focused on musical performances. Evidence is focused on video recordings of performances.
Articulation of Learning: Children should be able to articulate their learning in music. Children may demonstrate their learning through performance, verbally or via a musical outcome in order to do this.
Value of Music: At Cottesmore we recognise that music can be excellent subject for developing other non-musical skills. E.g. team work, confidence, language, pattern recognition, etc.. However, we believe that music is intrinsically a valued subject which should be taught in its own right and for its own sake.
Delivery
Music teaching is currently delivered by a specialist music teacher in Yrs 2-6. Using a specialist for this subject takes music out of the classroom, so activities are shared with class teachers to enable music to be embedded and sustained during the week in the general classroom. Music is taught for approximately 1 hr per week. In addition to this singing takes place in the classroom at other times during week (particularly at key stage 1 & EYFS) and at weekly 15 min singing assemblies. In Yr 4 music is delivered by specialist from Create Music’s Soundmakers programme.
Musical performances and celebrations
Music is a central part of school life at Cottesmore. Performances take place at regularly at masses and music concerts. Children regularly perform at hymn assemblies, or other music assemblies during the year. The school takes part in the One Voice massed choir performance with Create Music and takes part in the Schools Parade at Brighton Fringe. Musical performance is used continually as a tool to bring the school community together.
Co-curricular music:
Small group and individual instrumental lessons are available to children at the school. Funding for these lessons is available from Create Music for children who qualify for benefit related FSM and other benefits. Instrumental lessons are promoted during classroom music lessons, where children will learn about the instruments they could learn at school, or at local music centers. Visiting instrumental music teachers put on demonstration assemblies to raise the profile of the instruments they teach. Peripatetic teachers are provided by West Sussex Music and Rocksteady Currently we offer lessons on piano, keyboard, guitar, drum kit, violin, and brass. Other alternative instrumental learning is signposted to local out of school music centers.
Ensembles Choir: We run a weekly KS2 choir as a free before school club. The choir will lead singing at events and assemblies, and takes part in high profile performances in the community and with other schools. School Orchestra: We run a weekly KS2 orchestra as a free before school club. The orchestra is open to all pupils.Mass Choir: Mass choir is a initiation only choir for the school’s best singers. It takes the lead singing at school masses.
Live Music Experiences:
Authentic live performances make music real for children learning music and inspire them to become musicians themselves, or foster a love of music. Peripatetic teachers offer music demonstrations and assemblies to the school during the year. The school music teacher is a professional performer and offers regular live music performances on the instruments he plays. Children are encouraged to perform instruments they learn as part of music lessons, and can often feature in hymn assemblies.
Music in the Community
We are active in the local music Hub, attending music network meetings, and building up links with other local music coordinators. We attend termly Music Hub advisory group meetings. Cottesmore takes part in local multi-school performances both with other Brighton schools and the Diocese.
Instrumental Resources
The school has the following instrumental resources which are used throughout our instrumental learning. Where possible we are aiming to build up class sets of each instrument type so that children can learn any instrument together in class. We continue to develop our instrumental and music technology resources from school funds and also with support of the PTA and donations from parents Resources and year acquired if known below
· Recorders: set of 60 + spares
· Ukuleles: set of 32
· Xylophones: Mixed set of 32 small glockenspiels as well as large tenor and bass Xylophones.
· Keyboards: 17 with keyboard stands and stools
· Djembes: set of 32, various sizes. Various tuned and untuned percussion
· Boom whackers
· Digital Piano
· Upright Piano (library)
· Grand Piano (Hall)
· Samba Kit
· Guitar Amps
· PA System
· School ipads are used regularly in music lessons for recording work, garage band and appraising tasks.
Music Subject Development
We have a Music Subject Development plan, which includes yearly action plans as well as long term subject development goals.
Teaching Space
We have a dedicated music room at school. This gives us a large open plan space for teaching music away from other classrooms and with resources ready to use. We also use the school hall, and outside areas on the field and Forest School area for louder musical activities. We have a large hall which is used for singing assemblies and performances.
Subject specific national guidance
We have revised our music provision to be in line with the reflect the aims of the Model Music Curriculum and the National Plan for Music Education 2022. Our provision far exceeds the statutory requirements of the National Curriculum for Music.
Our provision meets the expectations of the Model Music Curriculum, although we have adapted specifics to suit our own pupils and teaching staff.
IMPACT
· Confident performers, who have experienced learning a wide range of instruments but with time to have in depth musical learning.
· Able singers, who feel confident using their voice
· Knowledge and understanding of music from many cultures, instruments and performers.
· Creative musicians, who can develop their own musical ideas in improvisations and compositions.

Science
National Curriculum [2014]: The Purpose of Science
A high-quality science education provides the foundations for understanding the world through the specific disciplines of biology, chemistry and physics. Science has changed our lives and is vital to the world’s future prosperity, and all pupils should be taught essential aspects of the knowledge, methods, processes and uses of science. Through building up a body of key foundational knowledge and concepts, pupils should be encouraged to recognise the power of rational explanation and develop a sense of excitement and curiosity about natural phenomena. They should be encouraged to understand how science can be used to explain what is occurring, predict how things will behave, and analyse causes.
‘It is important to view knowledge as sort of a semantic tree – make sure you understand the fundamental principles, i.e. the trunk and big branches, before you get into the leaves/details or there is nothing for them to hang on to.’ Elon Musk
Science Curriculum at Cottesmore
At Cottesmore, we recognise that science is an important aspect of our everyday lives. Science learning is vital to our world’s future success. As a school we wish to prepare our pupil’s for life in an ever changing and increasingly scientific and technological world. We are committed to providing the pupils with tools and experiences to be able to understand new technologies, their health and other important aspects of life, such as impact on our environment and how our choices influence the world around us. We place science learning in relevant contexts, for example, we identify plants that grow in our school environment, allowing children to see science in familiar settings. In year 1, children name, identify and observe plants and trees on the school grounds. These specific species are also on the Knowledge Organisers for them to make clear links with. Our children will confidently be able to make sense of the world, by using their scientific knowledge and understanding, gained from carefully structured science lessons. We are preparing our pupils for future scientific study by building strong foundations to help them in later life. We want them to have growth mind-sets, so they can enjoy science learning and tackle challenges they face daily.
We want to inspire the children to use their scientific knowledge, to make a difference in the world. They can be whatever they want to be: a science teacher, a geologist, an astronaut, a biochemist, a psychologist, a doctor, an engineer or a forensic scientist. The options are endless! They will be exposed to learning about different scientists, who have had a positive impact on the world, as we know it today.
We have deliberately created a knowledge rich curriculum and have defined the essential knowledge that pupils need to be educated citizens, introducing them to the best of human creativity and achievements. We have spaced knowledge, skills and concepts so that there is coherent flow to allow our learners to gradually build toward mastery and fluency. Topics are carefully sequenced across year groups to allow opportunities for children to make links and build their understanding of scientific concepts and skills in a wide variety of contexts. Links between topics have been identified, so that learning connects into a web of knowledge. We have defined expectations at key end points so we can assess the progress the children are making. We use knowledge organisers, detailing the key knowledge, vocabulary and key scientists related to the topic. The children take part in memorable scientific experiments and explorations designed to develop their curiosity about the world. They have the opportunity to use a wide variety of scientific resources related to their topics; good quality resources are key. We use our Forest School to give the children hands on practical experiences, enabling them to be curious, independent and inquisitive within a safe familiar environment. They will be able to develop their confidence, teamwork skills, resilience and problem-solving skills all whilst learning the wonders of the world. They will be able to discover new things, through specific STEM opportunities.
We want the children to be immersed in science, making cross curricular links and confidently use scientific vocabulary accurately to express their ideas. Science at our school links to all aspects of the wider curriculum. We link our science lessons to PE, history, geography and fair-trade/eco. For example, in History in Year 3 they learn about the Stone Age, while learning about rocks and fossils in Science and Year 5 learn about plants and animals in the rainforest in Geography, linking to animals and plants studies in science. Our science lessons encourage children to have the respect, thankfulness and pride in living things and the world God has created. Knowing that God has a special plan for all of us is at the heart of our learning and therefore we should all make the most of all learning opportunities. We want our children to dare to dream and always have hope in what they can achieve as scientists.
What Science topics do we teach?
At Cottesmore we take pride in the science opportunities we provide. The curriculum enables children to gain key scientific knowledge through explicit teaching and practical experiences. Science is broken down into the three mains strands of Chemistry, Biology and Physics. Children have the opportunity to develop and build on their skills in these three areas across all year groups.
At the start of each topic, teachers explain the ‘Big Idea’ to engage the children’s minds and evoke critical thinking when questioned on their existing knowledge and what they want to find out. It also enables children to make links in their learning. Each learning sequence is carefully planned to ensure the relevant key features of scientific enquiry have been taught, and children are provided with a Knowledge Organiser with all key information covered, including key vocabulary that is explicitly taught within lessons.
In Early Year, children are taught to understand the world around them, knowing similarities and differences between the natural world around them and contrasting environments, drawing on their experiences. Books are at the centre of Science in Early years, linking what they have read to the world they live in. They explore the important processes and changes in the natural world, looking at seasons and changing states of matter. In Key stage 1, topics cover the main disciplines of science: biology and chemistry. We teach the children the big idea of each discipline, introducing the foundational concepts of living things and matter. Building on their knowledge from Early Years, KS1 continues to build on knowledge of materials and uses of materials, animals including humans and their habitats and plants. They use Forest School to explore familiar contexts and build their observational skills from the world around them.
The children are first introduced to physics in year 3 in the topics ‘Light’ and ‘Forces’, where they first meet the concept of energy. Throughout year 4, 5 and 6 they build on the concepts of energy by learning about sound, electricity, forces and Earth and Space. In Year 6 they revisit the topic of ‘light’ to reinforce previously taught concepts and deepen their understanding. Many topics are covered more than once on their science journey through the school, ensuring knowledge in embedded and built upon and key links are made.
Click the image to view a larger version
In Key Stage 2 children develop their understanding of biology, all years in KS2 cover the topic Animals including humans. In lower key stage two they start by learning about nutrition, the skeleton and the digestive system, as they move into upper key stage two, they look at this topic in more detail building on previously taught concepts. For example human life cycle, ageing and the functions of the heart. They begin to create their own hypothesises and predictions creating experiments to test their theories. Throughout their science journey at Cottesmore, children begin to build an understanding of what it means to be ‘eco’ and how science plays a part in this. The children see how science effects the world around us and with our Key Scientist, see the impact that people have already made. The children are inspired to take their learning and explore the positive changes they can make to our world, using the knowledge they learn in these lessons. We have built eco links into lessons and have developed, alongside our eco lead, an eco-topic on carbon literacy for KS2. This further educates the children on important current affairs happening in our world and what they can do to make a difference.
Science skills, knowledge and concepts are taught together and within the context of a real place so that children learn the importance and spark an intrigue in how science fits in the world around them. We want children to understand the importance of learning the key knowledge in order to understand the skills needed for scientific enquiry and that these three learning stems are not isolated but are connected in order to form a full scientific foundation. Throughout the school, children study key scientists linked to their topics, these demonstrate the amazing discoveries leading researchers have made and the impact these have had on our world and the way we live.
Cross curricular- books are linked to each science topic to highlight science in stories and create cross curricular links to other subjects. We believe that learning is more memorable when it is linked to stories, and so we use stories as a vehicle for teaching science knowledge.
How is Science taught at Cottesmore?
We recognise science as its own subject with its own discipline and, as a result, a science lesson at Cottesmore is recognisable and different from other subjects.
A Science lessons ignites curiosity and discussions, it allows children to ask questions about the world they live in and why/how the world works.
We encourage the development of scientific skills through practical work including fair testing, observation, accurate measuring and repeating experiments. We encourage children’s natural curiosity through predicting, investigating, questioning and hypothesising. The children explore hands on science experiences in every topic and Forest School, given these practical experiences children get to see first-hand how science is all around us. Lessons are carefully planned so that they are firmly rooted in the local areas and the living things around us. For example Year 3 carry out a local study on the Seven Sisters, linking to erosion and why the cliffs are falling. Having this local experience lets children see what is happening in the areas near to them.
Teachers are equipped to deliver our curriculum through the provision of clear curriculum planning, where the knowledge, skills and concepts taught are clearly defined and links to prior learning are made explicit.
Click the image to view a larger version
Key scientific vocabulary is explicitly taught, through the use of quizzes and Frayer models. We encourage children to explain scientific concepts using the correct vocabulary both verbally and in their written work.
We build retrieval into lessons to enable children to consolidate and build on previously taught concepts, leading to a deep understanding of Science. This is done through using quizzes on previous lessons to assess understand and plug any gaps. Clear strands run throughout the school, starting in Reception and are built upon every year, therefore when children leave Cottesmore they are equipped with a broad and rich understand of numerous science concepts.
Pupils with special educational needs and/or disabilities have full access to our provision for science and teachers and other adults support these pupils so they access the same content as their peers. Experiments are planned so all children can access them, creating an inclusive science curriculum.
Enrichment In Science
We give children opportunities to immerse themselves in the excitement of Science outside of their lessons through assemblies and Science club. Children take their questions and hypothesis and get to experiment with these outside of the lesson. This furthers there understanding of key scientific concept as well as ignites a passion for learning science.
We plan opportunities for scientists to visit the school. Bringing professional equipment and deepen knowledge on various topics. The children then see how science can be used in the real world and spark that intrigue which might lead to the next generation of future scientists. Year 4 had a visit from Dr Francis, he taught them all about electricity, stretching their knowledge and deepening their understanding of this topic.
STEM boxes are used during science week for children to develop their understanding further through experimentation. Each year group is given an experiment to complete based on a scientific concept. For example, Year 3 tested their created and tested their own hypothesise on Forces (Spring topic) by make elastic cars and testing how far they could get them to go. Year 2’s STEM box looked at habitats (Autumn topic) where they created their own butterfly and designed a habitat that would camouflage the butterfly, hey then discussed why an animal might need to be camouflaged. These hand on experiences for the children are vital in creating a love of science and to get them questioning why and how they do experiments.

The Deeper Learning Journey

Sports Leaders
Sports Leaders are a group of children that show great enthusiasm and dedication in all aspects of sport. Their challenge is to develop sport within our school and inspire as many children as possible to engage in physical activity through fun, friendly and competitive competitions.
Sports leader meetings are held weekly with Mr. Buggy, to discuss activities that are being held within school that week. This is also an opportunity for the children to voice their opinions on school sport and create new ideas to encourage more children to engage in physical activity.
The role of a sports leader:• Encourage all children to get involved in sports.• Create new ideas to develop sport within our school.• Show sports leadership qualities such as team work, good listening skills, fair play and respect.• Follow and encourage others to live by the school games values:
Respect, Self-Belief, Honesty, Team Work, Passion and Determination.
• Help teach children certain skills within different aspects of sport.• Officiate different lunch time and intra-school competitions.• Take suggestions and ideas from their class about how sport can be improved within our school. • Help set up, get children involved, organise fair teams and record results from intra-school competitions.• Create and deliver key stage assemblies on upcoming sporting events. • Design posters to be placed around the school advertising sporting competitions and fundraising events.
Cottesmore Tag Rugby World Cup
Sports leaders were given the task to get as many friends as possible to sign up to our very own Rugby World Cup! We then fairly chose the teams, drawing them out of a hat and organising regular, weekly fixtures as part of our Intra-School competition. Sports leaders helped with officiating and recording results.
Sport Relief Celebration
Sports leaders came up with the idea of organising a charity event for the whole school to take part in and raise money for a good cause. We decided to choose Sport Relief as a charity we could raise money for and we also wanted to make a donation to our school catholic charity that we support. Firstly children had a Try-Athlon event to try and earn as many points as possible for themselves. Children took part in different events that were run by the sports leaders and their results were recorded. To finish off our Sport Relief celebration, the whole school took part in a 1 mile fun run around our field. Each child was given the opportunity to dress up as their sporting hero and asked to kindly donate £1 to Sport Relief. Prizes were awarded to the best dressed children and these were chosen by our sports leaders. We also came up with the idea of having a main prize draw for anyone that could raise £5 or over. This proved to be hugely popular and enabled us as a school to raise close to £3000!
Olympic and Paralympic Celebration
Our school were keen to celebrate the Olympic and Paralympic games with a whole school celebration. Sports leaders decided to plan an Olympic week with lots of fun activities linked to the Olympic and Paralympic games. Children were divided up fairly and given an Olympic country to represent throughout this week. They could earn points from different challenges and these would be totalled up at the end of our celebration! To start our Olympic week, classes were asked to design Olympic flags and banners within their classes. During this day, each class was given 30 minutes to come and play Paralympic games with sports leaders. Children had a go at Boccia, Goal ball, Seated Volleyball and Guided athletics. All of these games are events at the Paralympics and our children got the chance to have a go! On Tuesday the children took part in our annual school sports day. On Thursday the children competed in Olympic events, with more opportunities to gain points for their countries. Finally at the end of the week, children travelled all around the world, going to different classrooms and having a go at various activities linked to many Olympic countries. We celebrated France by building the Eifel tower and learning about French cuisine (mainly snails)! Greece by learning about how the Olympic games first started. Italy by building famous landmarks including the Colosseum and the leaning tower of Pisa. USA by learning all about line dancing. Australia by having a go at aboriginal dot paintings and Brazil by making carnival masks and having a go at samba dancing!

Art
Art and Design
National Curriculum [2014]: The Purpose of Art and Design
“A high-quality art and design education should engage, inspire and challenge pupils, equipping them with the knowledge and skills to experiment, invent and create their own works of art, craft and design. Pupils should know how art and design both reflect and shape our history, and contribute to the culture, creativity and wealth of our nation.”
INTENT
Art & Design Curriculum at Cottesmore
At Cottesmore we believe creative thinking is an important attribute to individual development within the arts. Within art we offer a visual, tactile and sensory experience exploring the many facets of creativity. Art offers a unique perspective to understand and respond to the world we live in. It can challenge conceptions, develop new thinking, and nurture ideas. It is so much more than making a finished product. Art and design embodies some of the highest forms of human creativity. At Cottesmore our art engages, inspires, and challenges our children equipping them with knowledge and skills to experiment, invent and create. As children progress in art we offer insight to creative thinking and understanding of art and design. We explore how art has contributed to our cultures, shaped our history and how to inspire and influence the modern world. We aim to promote a lifelong interest and enjoyment in the visual arts in the broadest sense.
Children study the work of other artists and unpick the skills, techniques and ideas and use these as inspiration for individual outcomes. This aspect of art at Cottesmore builds student thinking and development through exploration of other cultures, allowing them to question things and wonder about art and design as well as enjoy art on an aesthetic level.
We have a specialist art teacher and a designated art room, which children use in weekly lessons. They explore the seven core strands/concepts in art: form, drawing, pattern, texture, printmaking, painting, collage and colour. We take advantage of the rich artistic and cultural opportunities our city offers.
Learning Art and Design at Cottesmore not only prepares the children for studying the subject at secondary school but inspires them to understand the relevance of the subject in the wider community as well as opportunities in the creative industry as a career.
What Art and Design topics do we teach?
Art is taught in 6 weekly topics, with each year group completing 4 topics over the year. Our approach has a strong emphasis on the process of designing and making. Children explore and develop ideas, often using their sketchbooks and learn new skills and processes to enable them to express and develop their ideas.
Through drawing, painting and sculpture children share their ideas, experiences and imagination. Designed around a strong cultural brief, we develop a wide range of art and design techniques using colour, pattern, texture, line, shape, form and space. Children gain understanding about the work of a range of artists, craft makers and designers, they are able to describe the differences and similarities between different practices and disciplines, in order to make links to their own work.
The making part will sometimes be individual, or in partners or small groups. Children evaluate and reflect on what they and their peers have done through guided discussions, exploring ways of developing their work. The teacher gives verbal feedback during sessions and supports the children in finding the next steps in their learning.
In Year 2 pupils start to expand on the core art skills explored in Year 1. Projects are again linked to curriculum topics to support and expand knowledge whilst further developing skills in drawing, colour, texture, form, printing and pattern.
As children move into Key Stage 2 they begin to hone artistic skills through observational drawings linked to past and contemporary artists and art movements. Most projects link to curriculum themes, artist copies initiate research using a variety of media which are revisited through skills development before children start to design their own outcomes based on skills and knowledge learned. This independent creativity supports artistic ability and growth in the creative arena.
We study an ‘Artist of the Month’ across the school and children learn about the history of art, developing a clear sense of chronology and where artists fit into the bigger picture of Art.
IMPLEMENTATION
At Cottesmore we recognise the importance of practical learning and, through art, children have the opportunity to develop as artists, designers and craftsmen researching historical and contemporary skills and areas surrounding art and design. Skills progression is woven through our curriculum. Numeracy has an integral role in art and design, children are taught connections to mathematics and physics when exploring form, scale, proportion layout, composition and structure. Key phrases are evidenced and utilised making connections to literacy and language development. This helps children develop appropriate vocabulary by introducing and modelling technical vocabulary specific to art and art materials and processes.
We value talk and encourage children to ask questions, to comment on similarities and differences, to make comparisons, name and classify art. We build in opportunities for children to explain their intentions. We value children’s ideas and representations allowing children to produce individual, unique pieces of work not adult determined. We provide opportunities for children to play with ideas and talk about them.
This is achieved by allocating time to experiment, practise, repeat, re-visit and consolidate skills and providing a limited range of quality materials which children can grow familiar with. There is always time to reflect on the work that has been done and by providing quality stimulus using artifacts, objects, and a wide range of images.
Core learning for each topic is carefully chosen and knowledge organisers are used to support learning and retention of knowledge, as they are constantly used and revisited to ensure children remember knowledge over time. Children are taught about great artists and art movements and develop their understanding of the history of art timeline. We have our own kiln which allows children to work with clay and develop their modelling skills.
Challenge in Art & DesignUsing a clear progression of art based skills children are taught to develop and achieve more from their Art lessons. When children arrive confident and proficient in the learning, they are encouraged to deepen their understanding and extra challenges are provided to go deeper with their learning.
IMPACT
In accordance with the National Curriculum, progress in art is defined by practical application, the development of skills and knowledge. Therefore we have identified the 6 areas of art and design and woven these skills into all topics throughout Key Stage 1 and Key Stage 2. Children develop fine motor skills and tactile properties through experience and memory recall.
In line with our whole-school approach to learning, Cottesmore Art lessons are always adapted to the needs, knowledge and understanding of each class. Should children show a lack of understanding in lessons, learning is quickly adapted to suit their needs. Children and classes who show themselves to be more capable in certain subject areas are encouraged to further develop their skills and knowledge, for example through skill progression and use of advanced processes. Teachers use formative assessment to check what has been learnt and that learning has been remembered and achieved. It is used by teachers to provide feedback, to adjust teaching and learning and to identify pupils falling behind in the learning journey. At key points across and within the Key Stages, we use summative assessment to check pupils’ knowledge in the form of teacher led activities set against the 7 key skills in art and design.

Computing
Computing
National Curriculum[2014]: Computing A high-quality computing education equips pupils to use computational thinking and creativity to understand and change the world. The core of computing is computer science, in which pupils are taught the principles of information and computation, how digital systems work, and how to put this knowledge to use through programming.
INTENT
Computing Curriculum at Cottesmore Statement of IntentAt Cottesmore we want our children to be fluent in their understanding of technology. We want our children to know how technology impacts the world around them and importantly, how to stay safe whilst using this technology. At Cottesmore we strive to model and educate our pupils to use technology positively, responsibly and safely. As the digital world around us is ever-changing and expanding, we aim to equip our children with the knowledge and influence they need to begin to navigate the future pathways of this digital age, in secondary school and beyond.
Students learn the three main strands of computing: information technology; computer science coding and digital literacy. Units have been taken and adapted from the NCCE Teach Computing scheme. In EYFS and KS1, our children also learn key digital skills, such as mouse control and early coding, using Busy Things and Barefoot Computing. Our children are given opportunities to explore platforms to enhance IT skills, such as creating Stop Motion Animations, exploring physical systems by coding Micro:bits, as well as creating and understanding digital drawing packages. Coding projects offer our children creative freedom, from learning simple skills in Scratch to increasingly complex game building. Our computing curriculum is designed to be fun, engaging, progressive and coherent for all our children, with emerging cross-curricular links.
It is through these strands that our children become competent and skilled users of technology, understanding the ways in which it can influence and bolster our everyday lives. We strive to inspire future Scientists, Engineers and digital pioneers by allowing our children the chance to dream.
What Computing topics do we teach? Computing at Cottesmore is a discrete subject and is taught by a specialist Computing teacher.
In Key Stage 1 children start by developing their digital skills and knowledge with a focus on logging in to different platforms, navigating devices and mouse control. They learn what multimedia is and how to use different media types to create their own comic adventures using Book Creator.
As children move into Key Stage 2 our Computing curriculum advances with them. Children cover media topics such as creating Video Trailers in Year 3, build websites looking at HTML and webpage features in Year 4 and record Podcasts in Year 6, all of which link to the issue of Climate Change.
Coding at Cottesmore spans all year groups, beginning with basic sequencing in Year 1, through to an introduction to Python in Year 6.
IMPLEMENTATION
How is Computing taught at Cottesmore?We recognise Computing as a subject of its own. It is mostly taught by a specialist Computing teacher. Our curriculum has been created using some of the units given by the STEM NCCE scheme, as well as being created using the knowledge of the specialist teacher themselves and the consideration of children’s own capabilities. Lessons include unplugged learning, away from devices and technology; using iPads, often for topics such as Video or Photo editing; and units using the Computer suite, often for web-based lessons. As a result of this, Computing at Cottesmore is recognisable and different from other subjects. We give children the opportunity to develop their use of digital technology, teaching them valuable digital skills, readying them for secondary and beyond.
What does a Computing lesson look like at Cottesmore?
★ Computing at Cottesmore is often taught using digital devices.
★ Children’s digital skills are clearly progressed across the year.
★ Knowledge and skills have a clear progressive pathway across the school.
★ There is often a buzz of excitement as children engage in their lessons, create new programs or campaign video trailers.
★ Children are encouraged to collaborate and share their digital knowledge with each other.
Online safety is woven into lessons, from educating children about game and app age ratings to how to keep personal information private through to the consequences of online bullying and ways to behave when we are in the online world, whatever the device or circumstance. Children are taught the Online Safety mantra of Zip It, Block It, Flag It, to help them understand how to stay safe and report concerns.
Zip It, Block It, Flag It!
Trusted Adults & Helping Hands
In our EPR lessons, children learn to use their Helping Hand to name 5 adults they know and trust. In Computing we use our Helping Hands to understand who children can speak to about issues they experience online.
Click image above to view the video
Challenge in Computing
Through a clear progression of skills children are taught to thrive and achieve more from their Computing lessons. When children arrive already confident and proficient in the learning, they are encouraged to deepen their understanding and find ways to push themselves further with their learning. These children are often called upon to become the digital helper for the lesson, being shown how to follow the ‘driver vs navigator’ way of assisting others, ensuring they are able to explain their knowledge and the steps needed to achieve a similar level of understanding.
IMPACT
At Cottesmore, children progress in Computing by following and implementing small tasks, all of which help to progress and build their skills and knowledge. In Year 1, children begin their multimedia learning journey by learning to manipulate tools, add photos, videos and voice recordings on Seesaw, the learning platform used for homework and for evidencing the Computing curriculum. By the end of year 6, children independently make choices on the type of software or hardware needed to best present information, having experienced a range of software tools in their journey through the school.
In line with our whole-school approach to learning, Cottesmore Computing lessons are always adapted to the needs, knowledge and understanding of each class. Should children show a lack of understanding in lessons, learning is quickly adapted to suit their needs. Children and classes who show themselves to be more capable in certain subject areas are encouraged to further develop their skills and knowledge, for example by adding variables such as score counters or timers into basic games they are building.
Learning in Computing is seen as a journey, through children’s whole-school journey, as well as within each year group. Before building a complex game using block code, children learn sequencing through unplugged activities, they learn how to read and create flow charts, growing their programming knowledge from simple animations to complex games involving subroutines and variables.

Digital Leaders
Digital Leaders are a group of pupils who are elected to support the use of and to further develop Computing and Technology throughout the school.
Annually, children are given the opportunity to create a digital presentation that shows why and how they feel they can make difference to Computing in our school in addition to showing of their skill set. Decisions are then made from this.
Digital Leaders meet weekly, with Mr Cutting, where they are given training and support to develop specific areas of Computing expertise. These areas can be pupil led or may be around a new piece of hardware or software.
Digital Leaders:- Help other children with computing problems- Take lunchtime clubs, passing on their computer skills to others- Creating digital content for others such as digital books, simple programs,- Presentations for learning hints and tips etc.- Creating content for display within the school.- Create and deliver key stage assemblies on computing topics including E-Safety- Organise school competitions with a digital content.- Keeping the computer suite neat and tidy.- Taking suggestions from the class about ways the children think computing might be improved within the school.

Forest School
What is Forest School at Cottesmore?
Cottesmore Forest school ethos believes in a child’s fundamental right to play and within that play children have a right to access the outdoors (and in particular a woodland environment); the right to access risk and the vibrant reality of the natural world and the right to experience a healthy range of emotions through all the challenges of social interaction, in order to build a resilience that will enable continued and creative engagement with peers and their own potential. It is an approach to education that makes use of the outdoor environment to create a unique learning vehicle.
Why is Forest School important?
Forest school sessions provide increasingly diverse opportunities for children to benefit from a supportive curriculum that can help children build positive values and attitudes about themselves, about learning and the environment they live. In our modern lifestyles, fewer children play outside and screen time is an on-going controversy for many parents. Lockdown highlighted to us all how important it is to have access to outside space and nature. The time spent in Forest School is aimed at balancing this sociological change and igniting the passion for the outdoors in children at an early age. Children are given appropriately challenging and achievable tasks that build their confidence, skills and independence and are given time to thoroughly explore their thoughts, feelings and relationships. This time and reflective practice develop inter and intra-personal skills, which are well documented as being directly linked to learning skills.
Forest School in action at Cottesmore.
Woodland Trust Award
Over the last two years, Cottesmore Forest School has proven a sustainable approach to operating in a natural environment, planted over 100 trees and created memories for all children within the school. As a result of our on-going dedication and awareness, we have achieved the silver award from the Woodland Trust. Going forward, we aim to plant more trees, reduce school emissions and begin a composting system in order to achieve our gold award.This year we have planted a ‘Tree for the Jubilee’, in conjunction with the ‘Queen’s green canopy’ and English Woodlands.
